checked_sources: Kane et al. 2017 (full text, Europe PMC PMC6123891)
Pineda 2005 (full text PDF, author's UCSD lab copy, read via WebFetch)
Hobson & Bishop 2017 (full text, Europe PMC PMC5383811)
evidence_location: Kane 2017 glossary entries 'Alpha rhythm' ('Amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 µV in the adult'; activities in the alpha band differing 'as regards their topography and/or reactivity ... for instance: the mu rhythm') and 'Mu rhythm' ('Rhythm at 7–11 Hz ... Amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 µV'). Pineda 2005 section 1.1 (ICA sentence) and section 2.3 ('amplitude or power in the classical alpha rhythm tends to be larger than in mu rhythms', citing Storm van Leeuwen et al. 1976). Niedermeyer 1997 abstract ('found with scalp EEG in a minority of subjects but there is good reason to presume that all healthy adults have this rhythm'). Hobson & Bishop 2017 section 1 (2.9% Schnell & Klass [ref 12]; 14% of 500 healthy male adults, Gastaut et al. [refs 13, 14]; 'around half' by power spectral analysis, Kuhlman [18]; 60% of 54 participants by coherence, Schoppenhorst & Brauer [19]).
quote: new and more sophisticated techniques, such as independent component analysis (ICA), have shown that mu rhythms are found
discrepancy: All numbers and attributions are in the sources. Two small differences of condition: (1) 'of the 1950s': Hobson & Bishop write 'In the 1950s, the mu rhythm was thought to be a rare phenomenon' and then give the 2.9% and 14% figures, but their reference list dates the 2.9% study (Schnell & Klass, ref 12) to 1966; only the 14% (Gastaut et al. 1959) is from the 1950s. (2) 'visually read' is not stated for those two studies; it is inferred from Hobson's contrast with Kuhlman 1978 ('rarely visually identified ... power spectral analysis revealed it in around half'). Minor: Kane defines mu as 7–11 Hz, not fully inside its 8–13 Hz alpha band, though Kane itself treats mu as an alpha-band activity distinguished by topography and/or reactivity. The last sentence (sections 7 to 9 run mu at section 5's alpha strength as an upper bound) is the site's own and is consistent with Pineda's amplitude comparison.
suggested_fix: Replace 'in the visually read EEG of the 1950s' with 'in the visually read EEG of the 1950s and 1960s' (or 'in early visually read EEG'); otherwise keep.
bibliographic_issues: None. All four DOIs resolve in Europe PMC with the stated journals, volumes, pages and years (Clin Neurophysiol Pract 2:170–185; Brain Res Rev 50:57–68; Int J Psychophysiol 26:31–49; R Soc Open Sci 4:160662).

checked_sources: Wolpaw et al. 2002 (full text PDF, course copy at classes.engineering.wustl.edu, read via WebFetch; curl refused by proxy)
Wolpaw & McFarland 2004 (full text PDF from neurotechcenter.org, pdftotext; PNAS and PMC pages blocked)
Pineda 2005 (full text PDF, author's UCSD lab copy, via WebFetch)
Kirkup et al. 1997 (abstract only, Europe PMC)
evidence_location: Wolpaw 2002 section 3.4 ('often display 8–12 Hz EEG activity' ... 'usually associated with 18–26 Hz beta rhythms'), section 3.2 (slow cortical potentials), section 2.3.1 ('Evoked inputs (e.g. EEG produced by flashing letters) result from stereotyped sensory stimulation provided by the BCI' versus spontaneous inputs), section 3.1 (VEPs from brief visual stimuli). Wolpaw & McFarland 2004 Methods, 'Control of Cursor Movement' (p. 17850): 'amplitudes in a mu (8–12 Hz) or beta (18–26 Hz) rhythm frequency band over the right and left sensorimotor cortices', 'large Laplacian filter ... from two locations over sensorimotor cortex (C4 on the right and C3 on the left)'; Methods 'Users': 68, 22, 40 and 25 sessions at 2–4 per week, users A, B and D with 228, 28 and 47 prior one-dimensional sessions. Pineda 2005 section 3.3: 'subjects learned to control mu rhythms within 3–10 h of training'. Kirkup 1997 abstract: switching 'without prior learning' via alpha increases 'when people close their eyes for more than 1 s'; 'a majority, perhaps in excess of 90%, of the adult population'.
quote: amplitudes in a mu (8–12 Hz) or beta (18–26 Hz) rhythm frequency band over the right and left sensorimotor cortices
discrepancy: Every number is in a source, but the sentence links '3–10 hours of training' (Pineda 2005, for learning to control the mu rhythm) directly to the two-dimensional cursor control of Wolpaw & McFarland 2004, which took 22 to 68 daily sessions at 2 to 4 per week, and three of the four users had prior one-dimensional training (up to 228 sessions, 91 h). Wolpaw 2002 (section 3.4.1) likewise says most users 'acquire significant control within 2–3 weeks' of 40 min sessions. Also: the 2004 study used large-Laplacian derivations centred on C3 and C4 from a 64-electrode cap, not bare C3/C4; 'posterior alpha' is not stated in Kirkup's abstract (it says 'the alpha component of the EEG spectrum'); and Wolpaw 2002 classes P300 as an 'independent' BCI (it does not use the body's normal output pathways) while still calling it an evoked, stimulus-driven input, so 'need a stimulus' is right but 'dependent BCI' would not be.
suggested_fix: Split the training statement: 'learned to a usable level in 3–10 hours of training (Pineda 2005), and, with weeks of further practice, used for two-dimensional cursor control from derivations centred on C3 and C4 (Wolpaw & McFarland 2004: 22 to 68 sessions at 2 to 4 per week)'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Clin Neurophysiol 113(6):767–791; PNAS 101(51):17849–17854 (confirmed on the PDF); Brain Res Rev 50:57–68; Med Biol Eng Comput 35(5):504–509 all match.

Literature search: WebSearch (two queries) and a Europe PMC query for travelling waves with brain-computer/brain-machine interface, neurofeedback or operant conditioning
evidence_location: Takahashi 2011 Methods ('100-electrode "Utah" array', 'tetraplegic individual') and Discussion ('the wave propagation speed ranged between 15 and 35 cm/s'; the abstract gives 10 to 35 cm/s for the earlier monkey studies). Rubino 2006 abstract ('information about the visual target to be reached was encoded in terms of both latency and amplitude of evoked waves'). Takahashi 2015 Discussion ('Current decoding algorithms for brain machine interfaces have ignored the spatial organization ... In principle ... we could invert these spike prediction models to decode movement parameters'). Dogadov 2024 abstract (optical brain-machine interface in mice; 'Trained mice learned to generate these Conditioned Waves'; 'traveling cortical waves ... can be subject to operant control'); bioRxiv lists four versions (v1 2024-09-14 titled 'Operant conditioning of cortical waves through a brain-machine interface', v2 to v4 2025 titled 'Goal-directed shaping of cortical waves') and no journal version; Europe PMC has only the preprint record. Muller 2018 'Travelling waves in neural systems' (macroscopic waves recorded with EEG or ECoG 'generally have propagation speeds from 1 to 10 metres per second'; mesoscopic 0.1–0.8 m/s) and 'Macroscopic travelling waves' ('Signal distortion by cranial tissues and volume conduction, however, pose substantial possible confounds for detection of travelling waves in EEG'). Alamia & VanRullen 2019 Introduction and 'BW traveling waves in resting-state EEG data' ('FW waves in human EEG when participants were attending to visual stimulation and BW waves when participants' eyes remained closed'; 48 participants, 1 min eyes closed) and 'Speed of traveling waves' (1 to 10 m/s macroscopic, 0.1 to 0.8 m/s mesoscopic). Srinivasan 1998 abstract ('predicting that electrodes within 10-12 cm can appear correlated'). The wavelength 0.15–0.35 m/s over 20 Hz = 0.75–1.75 cm is correct arithmetic (site's own; Takahashi's beta band was 15–30 Hz, filtered 10–45 Hz).
quote: Signal distortion by cranial tissues and volume conduction, however, pose substantial possible confounds for detection of travelling waves in EEG.
discrepancy: The negative finding stands: no human demonstration of volitional travelling-wave control or of a BCI driven by travelling waves was found. Europe PMC returns only the Dogadov mouse preprint and an unrelated device for tracking epileptic waves; web searches found only descriptive, modelling and decoding-in-principle work. One condition differs: Alamia & VanRullen's forward waves were measured while participants attended a visual stimulus (a flickering luminance sequence), and backward waves with eyes closed in a separate resting dataset, so 'changes with the eyes open or closed' slightly overstates it: the contrast is visual stimulation versus eyes closed. Nuances, not errors: Srinivasan's 10–12 cm is the distance within which volume conduction makes electrodes appear correlated (inflated coherence), which the claim glosses as blur; Dogadov v1 was itself titled an operant 'brain-machine interface', so a wave-driven BCI does exist in mice, which the claim already says.
suggested_fix: 'whose direction reverses between visual stimulation and eyes closed' instead of 'changes with the eyes open or closed'.
bibliographic_issues: None found. All seven DOIs resolve with matching journals, volumes and pages. Dogadov et al.: the claim's title and author order match bioRxiv versions 3 and 4 (version 1 had a different title and version 2 a different author order); still unpublished in a journal as of this check.

checked_sources: Pfurtscheller, Brunner, Schlögl & Lopes da Silva 2006, publisher PDF (Elsevier typeset, doi in metadata) from pub.ista.ac.at/~schloegl/publications/pfurtscheller2006.pdf; Table 1 is an embedded image on p. 156, extracted with pdfimages and read at 2x
evidence_location: Table 1, p. 156 ('Frequencies and band power changes of the most reactive bands displaying ERD/ERS measured at 3 electrode positions and 4 motor tasks'; rows s1 to s9, Mean, SD; columns Left hand, Right hand, Foot, Tongue × C3, Cz, C4 × %, Hz). All 24 means and SDs match: left hand −64.6/25.2, −56.8/14.7, −86.7/9.4; right hand −84.7/16.8, −58.3/18.4, −71.6/18.8; foot 89.3/116.8, −21.3/65.1, 112.7/140.8; tongue 145.2/128.9, 107.0/66.8, 133.6/160.5 (per-subject columns re-summed for left-hand C3 and foot C3 give the printed means). Methods p. 154: nine subjects (six female, three male, right-handed, mean age 26.2); arrow cue at second 3 for 1.25 s, imagery to second 7, 60 trials per task; 'Quantification of ERD/ERS': 'percentage power decrease (ERD) or power increase (ERS) in relation to a 1-s reference interval before the warning tone', trial-averaged; bands chosen from time-frequency maps (2 Hz bands, 6–42 Hz) as the alpha (mu) rhythm 'with the most significant band power increase or decrease ... at the central electrode positions C3, Cz, and C4'. Results p. 157: 'the electrode position overlaying approximately the hand representation area (electrode positions C3 and C4)'.
quote: percentage power decrease (ERD) or power increase (ERS) in relation to a 1-s reference interval before the warning tone
suggested_fix: No number needs changing. Three nuances worth a note: (1) the most reactive band was chosen per subject, per electrode and per task (the Hz column varies within a subject, 9 to 14 Hz), not one band per subject; (2) the values come from Hjorth source-derivation (Laplacian) signals on a 60-electrode grid with about 2.5 cm spacing, not from monopolar C3, Cz, C4, which matters if the site models these as monopolar electrodes; (3) the 'foot' task was imagery of both feet; the SD row is the SD across the nine subjects.
bibliographic_issues: None. NeuroImage 31 (2006) 153–159, doi 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2005.12.003, authors Pfurtscheller, Brunner, Schlögl, Lopes da Silva, all confirmed on the PDF.
